title: When to Give People a Second Chance
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article lays out the conditions under which extending a second chance actually strengthens a working relationship rather than quietly damaging it. It rejects the idea that forgiveness should be automatic or free, insisting instead that the offending party must explicitly acknowledge the mistake and commit to not repeating it before trust is extended again. The piece warns specifically against the halfway measure of granting a second chance while still visibly distrusting the person, arguing that this doghouse dynamic guarantees underperformance and resentment. Its core insight is that a second chance only works when both leader and offender take real responsibility for the conditions that produced the mistake in the first place.
points: Forgiveness should never be free — it requires an explicit acknowledgment of the mistake and a real commitment not to repeat it.
Granting a second chance while still visibly distrusting the person is worse than either fully forgiving or ending the relationship.
Egregious mistakes rarely happen in a vacuum; both leader and offender typically share some responsibility for the conditions that produced them.
When trust is genuinely restored, people often perform better after a second chance, valuing the opportunity to prove themselves.
quotes: A willful mistake that erodes trust or seriously undermines credibility has to be forgiven.
Good leaders ask others to earn the ticket to hit replay and turn the consequences back to zero.
Even though leaders feel better about themselves when they forgive, forgiveness should not be free.
Those granted a second chance but held in the proverbial doghouse quickly become sour and disaffected.
The truth is that egregious mistakes don’t happen in a vacuum. Both parties usually play a role in the misstep, even if just creating the conditions for the violation to occur.
Screwing up happens, but a second chance can only occur through the forgiveness of a trusting leader.
